About: The Heating Curve — Ice on a Burner

Source

Topic
Thermal physics — specific and latent heat
Simulation
Heating curve of ice on a burner
Concept
Ice is heated from well below freezing. Heat goes in at a steady rate — watch where it shows up.
Serves
Distinguish heat that changes temperature (Q = mcΔT) from heat that changes state (Q = mL).
Inquiry
What does a thermometer in ice do when the burner is left on past 0 °C?
Misconception
“Adding heat always raises temperature.”

Pedagogy principles applied

Guided Inquiry

1 · Predict

The beaker holds 0.5 kg of ice at −20 °C. You switch the burner on and leave it on. The thermometer reads −20 °C, then climbs steadily. It reaches 0 °C — and the burner is still on. What does the thermometer do next?

2 · Watch

Press ▶ Play. Watch the thermometer climb from −20 °C to 0 °C, then watch what it does next while the energy counter keeps rising. In the molecular inset the lattice loosens and molecules break free, one by one.

3 · Compare the two lengths

Look at the graph. Compare the length of the sloping bit on the left (ice warming from −20 °C to 0 °C) with the length of the flat plateau (melting at 0 °C). For 0.5 kg of ice, which of these is right?

4 · Read the curve

Two quantities cover it: Q = mcΔT on the slopes and Q = mL on the plateau. Same joules — but on the plateau they break bonds, which the thermometer cannot see.

Now the sliders are yours. Halve the mass: the curve shrinks horizontally, but the ratio stays — it is the substance, not the amount. Power only speeds the dot along Q; it does not stretch the plateau.

The Heating Curve

01

At a glance

A beaker of ice at −20 °C sits on a burner, with a thermometer in it. The burner pours in energy at a steady rate, and the sim plots the temperature against the energy supplied.

What you'll learn

  • How to read a heating curve, a graph of temperature against the energy supplied.
  • How to count the energy for each stage with Q = mcΔT and Q = mLf.
  • How the ice mass and the burner power each change what you see.
Ice on a burner. You set the burner power and the mass of the ice.

What's on screen

  • Beaker and thermometer: the contents and a big temperature reading at the top.
  • Molecular view (top-left inset): a patch of molecules, with a caption that names what they are doing.
  • Graph: temperature T against energy supplied Q. An amber dot marks where the beaker is now.
  • Readouts (sidebar): Thermometer and Energy supplied, and a Phase budget with the phase and the energies to warm and to melt.
See itOpen the sim with its opening values: 0.5 kg of ice and a 500 W burner, not yet switched on. Watch for: −20.0 °C on the thermometer, 0 J of Energy supplied, and the amber dot at the left end of the graph.

Fixed: the ice starts at −20 °C and the graph stops at +25 °C. The sim uses cice = 2100 J/(kg·K), cwater = 4186 J/(kg·K) and Lf = 334 000 J/kg. It models no heat loss to the air.

03

Warming ice costs Q = mcΔT

While the ice is below 0 °C, every joule goes into warming it. The energy needed is the mass times the specific heat times the temperature rise.

Q = m cice ΔT
cice = 2100 J/(kg·K) is the energy that warms 1 kg of ice by 1 K.

Here ΔT is the rise from −20 °C to 0 °C, which is 20 K. For the opening 0.5 kg, Q = 0.5 × 2100 × 20 = 21 000 J, or 21 kJ. This is the first number in the Phase budget.

Q is proportional to the temperature rise, so the first stretch of the graph is a straight line. The burner supplies 500 J each second, so the climb takes 21 000 / 500 = 42 s.

See itRaise the power to 2000 W and press Play. Watch for: Solid (ice) in the Phase readout and the thermometer climbing steadily from −20.0 °C as Energy supplied grows.
04

Melting holds the temperature at 0 °C while the energy keeps flowing

At 0 °C the ice starts to melt, and the thermometer stops rising even though the burner is still on. The energy no longer raises the temperature. It breaks the bonds that hold the molecules in the crystal.

Q = m Lf
Lf = 334 000 J/kg is the latent heat of fusion, the energy that melts 1 kg of ice at 0 °C.

For 0.5 kg this is 0.5 × 334 000 = 167 000 J, or 167 kJ. In the molecular view the lattice loosens and molecules break free one at a time. The caption counts the percentage melted, and the water level in the beaker rises.

On the graph this stage is a flat line at 0 °C. No ΔT appears in the formula, because the temperature does not change.

See itStart at 20 kJ with a 2000 W burner, just short of the 21 kJ it takes to reach 0 °C. Watch for: the thermometer holding at 0.0 °C, Melting (ice + water) in the Phase readout, and Energy supplied climbing past 21 kJ.
05

Melting needs about eight times the energy of warming

Divide the two energies. The mass m cancels, so the ratio depends only on the substance and on the 20 K climb.

Qmelt / Qwarm = Lf / (cice ΔT) = 334 000 / (2100 × 20) ≈ 7.95
The Phase budget shows this as Ratio (melt ÷ climb).

So the flat part of the graph is about eight times longer than the sloping part before it. Melting ice takes far more energy than warming it by 20 K, and the thermometer shows none of it.

Changing the mass rescales both energies together. Halve the mass to 0.25 kg and they become 10.5 kJ and 83.5 kJ, but the ratio stays 7.95.

See itSet the Ice mass to 0.25 kg. Watch for: the Phase budget at 10.5 kJ and 83.5 kJ with the ratio still 7.95×, and the graph's plateau label reading the same ratio.
06

Power sets the speed, and mass sets the scale

The graph is drawn against energy, not time, so the burner power does not change its shape. Power only decides how long each stage takes, through t = Q / P. For 0.5 kg, melting takes 167 000 / 500 = 334 s at 500 W, and 167 000 / 2000 = 83.5 s at 2000 W.

Mass scales every stage in proportion, since each Q has an m in it.

Ice masswarm to 0 °Cmeltratio
0.25 kg10.5 kJ83.5 kJ7.95
0.50 kg21 kJ167 kJ7.95
1.00 kg42 kJ334 kJ7.95

The sim fixes the graph's energy axis for the largest mass, 1.0 kg, so a smaller mass draws a shorter curve on the same axis.

See itSet the power to 2000 W with the default 0.5 kg, and press Play. Watch for: Energy supplied climbing about four times faster than at 500 W, while the Phase budget stays at 21 kJ, 167 kJ and 7.95×.
07

Melted water warms again, at about half the rate per joule

When the last ice has melted, the energy goes back into raising the temperature, now of liquid water. The rule is the same, Q = m cwater ΔT, with cwater = 4186 J/(kg·K).

Water holds about twice as much energy per kelvin as ice (4186 against 2100). Each joule therefore raises the temperature by only about half as much, and the last stretch of the graph is about half as steep as the first.

For 0.5 kg, warming from 0 °C to the graph's top of 25 °C takes 0.5 × 4186 × 25 = 52 325 J, about 52.3 kJ. The full run then totals 21 + 167 + 52.3 ≈ 240 kJ, and the burner stops there.

See itStart at 187 kJ with a 2000 W burner, just before the last of the ice melts. Watch for: the Phase readout changing to Liquid (water) and the thermometer rising again from 0.0 °C, more gently than it did for the ice.
08

Where it matters

  • Cold drinks. Melting 1 kg of ice absorbs 334 kJ. That is as much as warming 1 kg of water by about 80 K, so ice cools a drink far better than the same mass of 0 °C water.
  • Calorimetry problems. Before mixing ice and water, check each stage in turn: warm the ice to 0 °C, melt it, then warm the water. The heat lost by the hot side must cover them in that order.
  • Freezing releases heat. The same 334 kJ/kg comes back out when water freezes. Growers spray crops with water on frosty nights so that freezing keeps the buds near 0 °C.
Go deeper: why the temperature stays put

Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the molecules. During melting the supplied energy raises their potential energy, as the bonds of the lattice are pulled apart. The kinetic energy stays the same, so the thermometer reads 0 °C until the last crystal is gone. Boiling works the same way with a much larger latent heat, which this sim does not model.

09

Summary

In one line. This sim follows ice on a burner and tracks the temperature as the energy supplied grows, so you can see where each joule goes.

Key points

  • Warming at constant phase: Q = mcΔT. The ice stage needs 21 kJ for 0.5 kg.
  • Melting at 0 °C: Q = mLf = 167 kJ for 0.5 kg, with no temperature change.
  • The melt-to-warm ratio is Lf / (cice ΔT) = 7.95 for any mass.

Common mix-ups

  • "Adding heat always raises the temperature." During a change of state the heat goes into the bonds, and the temperature stays put.
  • "A stronger burner stretches the plateau." The graph is against energy, so power only changes how fast the dot moves along it.
  • "A bigger mass makes the plateau relatively longer." Mass scales both stages, so the ratio stays 7.95.

Things to try on your own

  • Predict the Phase budget for 0.8 kg of ice, then set the slider and compare.
  • Find the power at which melting 0.5 kg takes about 60 s, then check it with the Speed control.
  • Run a full cycle and read the Energy supplied when the run ends.
